Why can't BCA's caution reach harm that:
Point: Study 6 showed BCA's kind of caution can't fix this harm; Study 7 explains why.
On the slide: The three boxes say why we ran it, what it does, and how. We read BCA's code line by line, and used Study 6's saved critics and actors with exact values from simulation. No BCA was trained.
Why it matters: Before changing BCA, we needed the exact reason it fails. The next slide gives three reasons, straight from the code.
BCA reads and acts where the critic is r:
Point: BCA looks for errors in the wrong place, and its fix pushes in the wrong direction.
On the slide: One: BCA only checks the critic on rows that are in the data, and there the critic is accurate. Two: its only lever is a stronger pull toward the logged command, which says drive like the recorder, not stop at 80%. Three: that pull is capped at 1.5 times, and when BCA can't vouch for a command it adds no caution at all.
Why it matters: The critic is wrong only about commands the data never show. The next two slides prove that with the data.
The critic is right up to 80% and wrong:
Point: The trained critic thinks full throttle is fine when it actually costs a lot.
On the slide: The dark line is the true value of each throttle compared with holding at 80%. The orange line is the critic trained on the data with the gap. Up to 80% they match. Past 80% the truth drops to minus 0.46, but this critic says plus 0.06. The blue dashed critic, which saw the full data, gets it right.
Why it matters: The error sits only where the data are missing. BCA never checks there.
Cap the actor at 80% and it scores 101.8:
Point: This one wrong belief causes almost all the harm.
On the slide: The orange bar is the controller trained on the gapped data, in strong current: minus 14.3 points. The blue bar is the same controller with its commands capped at 80% while it runs: 101.8 points, better than the controller trained on the full data, at 84.6.
Why it matters: Everything else the controller learned is good. So the fix is narrow: correct the critic's value of past-80% commands, at the controller's own commands.
BCA acts where the critic is right:
Point: BCA's signal is read and used where the critic is already right, so it can't reach this harm.
On the slide: The left box says why: even the perfect harm signal, put in BCA's channel, won almost nothing back in Study 6. The right box says what has to change: read BCA's band at the controller's own command, lower the value it climbs, drop the 1.5 cap, and treat 'can't vouch' as maximum caution.
Why it matters: That is a new channel. Study 8 tests it.
Can caution reach the harm if it acts on:
Point: Study 8 tests a new way to apply caution, first with perfect information, then with BCA.
On the slide: Instead of pulling the controller toward the data, we lower the critic's value at the controller's own command by how much it is overrated there. The setup list shows the four parts: the perfect-information test, data-only rivals, a test of whether the harm itself can be seen, and BCA itself in Stage 2.
Why it matters: If even perfect information fails in this channel, no version of BCA can succeed. So we test that first.
Lower the value where the critic overrat:
Point: Before any results, this is how the new channel works.
On the slide: Card 1: the controller climbs the critic's value minus a penalty at its own command. Card 2: in this first test the penalty is the critic's exact error from simulation, as a best case. Card 3: the controls get the same strength of caution but untargeted: even pull, pushing less everywhere, and random penalties.
Why it matters: If the targeted penalty beats untargeted caution of the same strength, placement is what matters. The next slide shows it does.
The new channel wins back 94 of 99 point:
Point: With perfect information, the new channel fixes almost all the harm.
On the slide: Each bar is a controller's score in strong current. No caution scores minus 14.3. The exact-error penalty scores 79.7, winning back 94 of 99 points. Every untargeted control of the same strength stays below zero. The right error taken from the wrong state also fails.
Why it matters: The channel works, and only when the signal is in the right place. The question now is whether any real signal, BCA included, can supply it.
The rivals BCA must beat, and how the tr:
Point: These are the data-only signals BCA has to beat, defined before the results.
On the slide: The range hinge penalises throttles beyond the recorded range. Novelty signals measure how unusual a command is. The classifier ratio is a model's odds that a command came from the controller rather than the data. Two-head disagreement is how much the critic's two copies disagree. The bottom line explains the trace test.
Why it matters: If simple signals like these do as well, BCA adds nothing. The next slide shows how they do.
A perfect signal is cautious only where:
Point: A good signal wins back the harm without costing points where the missing commands are actually fine.
On the slide: The left bars show points won back in strong current. The right bars show points lost in a matching world where full throttle works. The perfect signal wins back 93.9 and loses only 1.3. The range hinge wins back 84.6 but loses 20.4. The others win back little.
Why it matters: The range hinge sets the bar for BCA. To beat it, BCA must be just as protective but cost less.
A trace of the stall in the data stayed:
Point: We could not build a test of whether BCA spots the harm itself, not just unusual commands.
On the slide: We kept 0.5 to 10% of the removed full-throttle rows. Left: the harm stays above 50 points up to 5%. Right: a data-only signal never separates the stalling world from the safe one, never reaching the 0.2 mark. Only three seeds, and the larger shares were added after a first look.
Why it matters: So here BCA can only show it flags unsupported commands. Proving it finds the harm itself needs a new test bed.
BCA's band, read at the actor's own comm:
Point: Stage 2 puts BCA's own uncertainty band into the new channel.
On the slide: Card 1: read BCA's band at the controller's own command and compare it with the logged command's. Card 2: the controller climbs the critic's value minus that extra width, uncapped. Card 3: the same band screens commands while the controller runs. The bottom row says the plain band missed and the weighted band passed three of four tests.
Why it matters: This version was pre-registered and you approved it. The next slide explains how detection is scored.
How BCA's detection is scored: four test:
Point: Four tests decide whether BCA's band flags the right commands.
On the slide: Direction: is the band wider at a bad past-80% command than at the same command capped at 80%? Size: is the extra penalty big enough to cancel the critic's mistake? Ranking: does a bad command score above a harmless one? Rivals: is BCA within 0.02 of the best data-only signal? Each must hold on average and in at least 4 of 5 seeds.
Why it matters: These were fixed in advance. Next is the first result.
BCA's band barely changes past 80%:
Point: BCA's plain band failed: it doesn't widen where the critic is wrong.
On the slide: The orange bar is BCA's plain band. It ranks bad commands above harmless ones 0.80 of the time on training states and 0.62 in strong current. The classifier ratio, a simple data-only signal, scores 0.99 and 0.90. The bottom row adds the size result: 0.0004 against a mark of 1, so the band barely changes past 80%. Calibration itself is fine.
Why it matters: The plan's declared fallback was a weighted version. That is the next slide.
With classifier weights, BCA's band flag:
Point: The weighted band passes, but mostly by borrowing the best rival's signal.
On the slide: The blue bars are the weighted band: 0.99 on training states and 0.86 in strong current. It is now wider at bad commands in every pair and every seed, and big enough to cancel the critic's mistake. But its weights come from the same classifier that scores 0.99 and 0.90 on its own, so in strong current BCA is slightly worse than that classifier.
Why it matters: Detection now works well enough to unlock the real test: does BCA's penalty win back return?
BCA flags the problem with weights; poli:
Point: The new channel works; BCA can flag the problem with help; whether it wins back return is still open.
On the slide: The bar counts eight checks so far: five met, two missed, one pending. The misses are the plain band and the trace test. The left box says why: the plain band barely changes, and the weighted one is no better than the classifier alone. The right box says what decides it now.
Why it matters: The policy test is running on seeds 0 to 4 and answers the question that matters.
Eight questions, eight answers (1 of 2):
Point: Studies 1 to 4 asked whether BCA's statistical promise holds, and found real problems.
On the slide: Code: matches the paper, one gap left. Shift: BCA today fails; row weights mostly fix it. Bank: it only holds with few rows per episode. Algorithms: two datasets fail on all four.
Why it matters: These made the promise more trustworthy, but none of them tested whether BCA improves learning. That's the second half.
Eight questions, eight answers (2 of 2):
Point: Studies 5 to 8 asked whether BCA helps the controller learn. Not yet.
On the slide: Study 5: BCA measured the wrong copy of the critic. Study 6: the harm is real, but BCA's channel can't reach it. Study 7: BCA checks where the critic is right. Study 8: a new channel works with perfect information; BCA needs classifier weights to flag the problem.
Why it matters: The honest summary: the promise is sounder, and we know what has to change, but no learning win yet.
What happens next, in order:
Point: Four steps, in order.
On the slide: One: the policy test on seeds 0 to 4, running now, compares BCA's penalty with the range hinge and matched controls. Two: the deployment check and full training. Three: the confirmatory run on fresh seeds 5 to 9, with every setting frozen. Four: a test bed where the harm itself is visible, and real benchmark data.
Why it matters: Only the fresh-seed run can support a claim. Everything before it is exploratory.
References:
Point: The papers behind each method in the deck.
On the slide: Each entry names the method it supports: conformal risk control, the D4RL benchmark, the learners TD3+BC, CQL, IQL and ReBRAC, WBCP, and importance weights under shift.
Why it matters: Use this if someone asks where a method comes from.
Definitions, code and open inconsistenci:
Point: Backup material, for questions only.
On the slide: The list shows what is in the appendix: terms, how a rule is judged, the code for each rule and for BCA's bank and dose, and where our write-ups disagree.
Why it matters: Skip in the talk; jump here if asked.
Words and symbols used throughout:
Point: The exact definitions behind the plain words in the talk.
On the slide: The score is the critic's error divided by BCA's predicted error size. The cut-off is the score BCA promises most rows stay under. Shift reweights rows. Rho measures how alike rows in one episode are; K is rows taken per episode.
Why it matters: Use for precise questions.
How is a rule judged?:
Point: How we decide whether a cut-off rule passed.
On the slide: The code counts, over many random banks, how often a rule's cut-off misses more than 10% of new rows. A rule is valid if that happens in at most 5% of banks. Declining to give a cut-off counts as a pass here.
Why it matters: This is the pass mark behind Studies 1 to 4.
What does every rule compute?:
Point: Every rule takes a bank of past errors and returns one cut-off.
On the slide: The code computes, exactly, the share of all held-out rows whose error is above the cut-off. The rules differ only in how they pick it.
Why it matters: Because the share is exact, each rule's success or failure is measured, not estimated.
Three kinds of guarantee:
Point: The rules promise different things.
On the slide: Marginal: right on average over banks. High-probability: right for at least 95% of banks. Posterior credibility: what WBCP promises. W-CRC: a weighted, average-risk comparison.
Why it matters: When comparing rules, compare the same kind of promise.
BQ‑CP: a posterior over the threshold:
Point: How BCA's current rule picks its cut-off.
On the slide: The code randomly reweights the bank many times and records where each reweighting crosses the 10% error line. The cut-off is the value 95% of those reweightings agree on.
Why it matters: This is the rule Studies 1 to 5 test.
How BCA builds its bank today:
Point: How BCA picks the held-out rows it calibrates on.
On the slide: It picks whole episodes, more likely if longer, then takes K evenly spaced rows from each, and trims extras at random.
Why it matters: Taking few rows per episode is the fix from Study 3.
How the calibrated width becomes a dose:
Point: How BCA's band becomes extra caution.
On the slide: The width is the cut-off times the predicted error size at each logged row. The dose turns it into a multiplier from 1 to 1.5. If BCA can't vouch for a row, the dose is 1: no extra caution.
Why it matters: That last rule is one reason BCA can't reach harm outside the data.
The hook: where the dose enters TD3+BC's:
Point: Exactly where BCA's dose enters training.
On the slide: The controller's loss reads the critic's first copy and adds the pull toward the logged command. BCA's dose multiplies that pull on each row.
Why it matters: This line is BCA's whole channel today, the one Studies 6 and 7 show can't reach the harm.
TD3+BC: the actor reads Q1, BCA calibrat:
Point: The code behind Study 5's finding.
On the slide: The controller follows the critic's first copy, Q1. BCA calibrates the smaller of the two copies. So BCA was checking a different number from the one the controller follows.
Why it matters: That mismatch is why Study 5 recommends measuring Q1.
Where do the write-ups disagree? (1 of 2:
Point: Places where our own documents disagree, listed so nobody is surprised.
On the slide: Each row gives the topic, the disagreement and the fix. None of them changes a result.
Why it matters: Being upfront about these builds trust in the rest.
Where do the write-ups disagree? (2 of 2:
Point: The rest of the documented disagreements.
On the slide: Same format: topic, disagreement, fix. None changes a result.
Why it matters: These are the clean-up list for the write-ups.
When missing data hide a trap, is there:
Point: Studies 1 to 5 checked BCA's promise. Now we ask the real question: does BCA's caution help a controller learn?
On the slide: We built a simulated task where we know every true value. We hid a trap: past 80% throttle, thrusters stall. Then we removed almost every past-80% example from the training data. The status bar says the test stopped before BCA ran, as planned, because extra caution of BCA's kind could not help.
Why it matters: The next slides build the task up step by step before any result.
The Gapped LQ world failed its own gate:
Point: Our earlier test world was too broken to test BCA, so we built a new one.
On the slide: The bars count how many of 5 seeds showed the loss sitting where data were thin. We needed 4. It never got above 3, in either attempt. The critic was wrong almost everywhere, not just where data were missing.
Why it matters: To test BCA we need a world where the critic is wrong only where data are missing. That's ThrusterChain, next.
The task: hold five floats at rest again:
Point: The task is to hold five floats still against a current and waves, using four thrusters, with as little throttle as possible.
On the slide: Left: five floats on springs, four thrusters between them, and water pushing every float the same way. Right: the trap. Push grows with throttle up to 80%, then falls. In a comparison world it keeps rising.
Why it matters: A good controller stops at 80%. The data will hide that fact. Next: what the controller sees and controls.
Four throttles in, thirteen numbers out:
Point: The controller sets four throttles and sees thirteen numbers.
On the slide: Left table: the four actions, one throttle per thruster, from minus 1 to 1. Right table: the observation, which is each float's position and speed, the strength of the current, and two numbers giving the wave's position in its cycle.
Why it matters: This is the standard Gymnasium interface, so any learning method plugs in. Next: how one step works.
Floats swing, water pushes, thrusters pu:
Point: Each step, three things move the floats: their own swing, the water and the thrusters.
On the slide: Card 1: each float swings and slowly settles, with weak springs linking them. Card 2: each thruster pushes two neighbouring floats, and past 80% its push drops. Card 3: the water pushes every float equally, a steady current plus a wave. There is no randomness at all.
Why it matters: Because nothing is random, we can compute the exact right answer for any state, which is what makes the test fair.
What is scored, how an episode starts, a:
Point: Lower cost is better, every episode is 100 steps, and scores are put on a 0-to-100 scale.
On the slide: The reward each step is minus how far the floats are from rest, minus a small cost for throttle. Episodes start with random floats, current and waves. Points: 0 means as good as the controller that recorded the data, 100 means as good as a hand-built controller that knows to stop at 80%.
Why it matters: Every result later is in these points.
Eight registered versions: two worlds ×:
Point: We test in four situations, and two of them are outside anything in the training data.
On the slide: The table lists the stalling world's four versions: normal conditions, strong current, big waves and big starting kicks. Strong current and big waves never appear in the data. A no-stall twin of each exists, where full throttle is fine.
Why it matters: Strong current is where the trap bites, because holding against it needs more than 80% throttle.
The data: one recording controller, then:
Point: We recorded data from one controller, then removed the examples that would reveal the trap.
On the slide: Card 1: the recording controller often uses full throttle when the water pushes hard. Card 2: 1,000 episodes of 100 steps, split into training, calibration and held-out data. Card 3: the standard D4RL rule removes the densest 15% of commands, which takes out 99% of the full-throttle examples.
Why it matters: The training data still visit the hard states, but almost never show what full throttle does there.
Fixed reference controllers set the poin:
Point: Two fixed controllers define 0 and 100 points; the others show what each kind of mistake costs.
On the slide: Each row is a controller; each column is a situation, with the raw score and the points in brackets. The recording controller is 0. The stall-aware controller is 100. The rising-thrust controller, which believes full throttle is fine, scores minus 54 in strong current.
Why it matters: That minus 54 is exactly the mistake a learner makes if it never sees the stall.
The learner: a critic rates, an actor pi:
Point: The learner has two parts: a critic that scores commands, and an actor that picks them.
On the slide: Card 1: the critic learns from the data how good each command is. Card 2: the actor picks commands the critic rates highly, while being pulled toward the commands in the data. Card 3: alpha sets how much the actor trusts the critic versus the data.
Why it matters: We train two critics, one on all the data and one on the data with the gap. Any difference comes from the missing examples.
BCA today: a calibrated band, turned int:
Point: Today BCA turns its uncertainty about the critic into a stronger pull toward the data.
On the slide: Card 1: BCA estimates how wrong the critic might be on each data row, its band. Card 2: a wider band gives a bigger multiplier, between 1 and 1.5. Card 3: that multiplier strengthens the pull toward the logged command on that row.
Why it matters: The question is whether that extra pull can undo the harm from missing data. The checks on the next slide test that.
Four checks, fixed in advance, before BC:
Point: We fixed four checks in advance. BCA is only judged if there is real room for it to help.
On the slide: Check 1: is the critic wrong where data are missing? Check 2: does that cost the controller points? Check 3: could caution of BCA's kind help, even placed perfectly? Check 4: is there enough statistical power? Each has a pass mark and controls that rule out other explanations.
Why it matters: If check 3 fails, BCA can't win in this setup however good its signal is. Next: the results.
The missing data cost 99 points in stron:
Point: The gap in the data causes real harm, and it shows up when conditions change.
On the slide: Blue bars: the controller trained with all the data. Orange bars: the controller trained with the gap. In normal conditions they are close. In strong current the gapped one falls to minus 14.3 points against 84.6, a 99-point loss. Removing random data instead costs almost nothing.
Why it matters: Checks 1 and 2 pass. The critic is wrong where data are missing, and it costs a lot. Now: can BCA's kind of caution fix it?
Caution of BCA's kind cannot win it back:
Point: Even placed perfectly, BCA's kind of caution wins back almost nothing.
On the slide: Each bar is a controller's score in strong current. The blue one uses the true harm to decide where to pull toward the data, information BCA could never have. It scores minus 7.6, barely different from even or shuffled caution. The dashed line at 84.6 is where we'd need to get. Only tripling the pull everywhere helps a little, and it hurts everything else.
Why it matters: Check 3 fails, so BCA's current channel cannot reach this harm.
The harm is real, but BCA's channel cann:
Point: The data gap causes real harm, but pulling harder toward the data can't fix it.
On the slide: The bar shows the four checks: two passed, one failed, one not reached. The left box says why: the pull acts on data rows, toward data commands, but in strong current the controller is far from both. The right box: a better signal alone won't help. The channel has to change.
Why it matters: That raises the question Study 7 answers: why exactly does BCA's channel miss?
Studies 5–8: does it help the actor?:
Point: Studies 5 to 8 ask whether BCA helps the controller learn, and so far it has not.
On the slide: Study 5, still with frozen critics, found BCA checks the wrong copy of the critic. Studies 6 and 7, in ThrusterChain, our simulated task, found the missing data cost 99 points in strong current, and BCA's extra pull toward the data can't win them back, because BCA checks where the critic is already right. Study 8 found a channel that works with perfect information; BCA's band only flags the problem once it borrows a classifier's weights.
Why it matters: The scorecard next puts all eight on one page.
The guarantee is sounder; there is no wi:
Point: BCA's promise is more trustworthy now, but BCA has not yet improved a learned controller.
On the slide: Card 1: studies 1 to 5 found four flaws in how BCA sets its cut-off, each with a fix. Card 2: none of those studies measured learning, and the only return number is one seed. Card 3: in ThrusterChain, extra pull toward the data wins back almost none of the 99 points the data gap costs. Card 4: penalising the value of the controller's own command wins back 94 with perfect information; BCA's band flags the problem only with borrowed classifier weights, and the policy test is running.
Why it matters: That's the whole talk in one slide. Next, study 1.
